svg.title: How thyroglobulin is read: surgical extent against radioiodine status
svg.desc: Schematic drawing the reading of thyroglobulin as a four-cell map: across, whether radioiodine was given; down, how much of the gland was removed, total thyroidectomy or lobectomy. Top left is total thyroidectomy with radioiodine: the line for an excellent response is a nonstimulated thyroglobulin - the one drawn while you are taking your tablet - below 0.2 ng/mL, or a stimulated thyroglobulin below 1, with negative imaging. All four response categories exist in this column, the data are fullest here, and the structural recurrence bands the guideline collects come from this column's population. Top right is total thyroidectomy without radioiodine: the same cell's line becomes below 2.5 ng/mL, a difference of more than tenfold and not a typographical error, because radioiodine clears the normal thyroid tissue the operation left behind, that tissue is still present when radioiodine was not given, normal tissue makes this protein too, and the baseline is simply higher; the structural recurrence figures for this column are lower overall than for the cell on its left. Bottom left is lobectomy without radioiodine: the excellent-response cell does not look at thyroglobulin at all, but at whether the contralateral lobe has a nodule, whether a biopsy of it was benign, and whether imaging shows abnormal nodes. The indeterminate response and biochemical incomplete response cells are written N/A in the guideline's own table, and the figure draws them as two hatched, crossed-out cells labelled N/A rather than supplying a number. On routine thyroglobulin after lobectomy the guideline says it is not recommended routinely, a conditional recommendation with very low certainty, and ultrasound carries the follow-up rather than the blood test. Bottom right is lobectomy with radioiodine: this cell does not exist in the table, because the guideline splits the reading into three columns, so it is drawn as a crossed-out empty box stating that the figure invents no line for it. The second part explains why the lobectomy column is not the same kind of thing. The 2022 systematic review reports the three situations separately: after lobectomy, 4 studies and 561 patients; total thyroidectomy without radioiodine, 5 studies and 751 patients; after total thyroidectomy and before radioiodine, 28 studies and 7,618 patients. Its verbatim conclusion on the first situation is quoted - "Following partial thyroidectomy, Tg measurement was not accurate for diagnosing recurrence or metastasis, or estimates were imprecise" - and it rates the quality of evidence as very low in every situation. A red-bordered cell records that the 30 ng/mL cutoff was not adopted: it was indeed proposed for lobectomy in 2016, in a single-centre cohort of 507 patients, none of whom had radioiodine, but the 2025 edition did not take it up. Beside it, a cell records that even in the two left-hand columns the first result is not the verdict: in a cohort of 299 patients, all of whom had total thyroidectomy and remnant ablation and nothing further, only 58% had reached their nadir by six months and 75% by twelve. The third part sets out the four response categories with their structural recurrence rates, in adults with differentiated thyroid cancer after total thyroidectomy and radioiodine - the people in the top left cell - as five range bands: excellent response 1 to 4%, and 0.2 to 2% for those who were low risk from the start; indeterminate response 5% to 15-20%; biochemical incomplete response 20 to 53%; and structural incomplete response drawn as a hatched band labelled "visible on imaging", because it is defined by local or distant metastases on imaging rather than by a percentage. The note records that the corresponding figures in the column without radioiodine are lower overall, and that these four cells describe where a patient is now rather than where they were placed at the start. Two cells then show the classification rewriting the starting category: in a cohort of 588 patients with median follow-up 7 years, persistent structural disease or recurrence ran at 3% in those initially low risk, 21% at intermediate risk and 68% at high risk, and after re-classification at an excellent response in the first two years the three became 2%, 2% and 14%; in a cohort of 506 patients with median follow-up 10 years the figures were 13%, 36% and 68%, falling to 1.4% in those reaching an excellent response. A note records that neither set matches the figures in the sister article on staging, 1.5%, 5.4% and 25%, because the endpoint definitions and the cohorts differ, and that the same category giving different percentages in different studies is itself why the starting category is not a verdict. The fourth part is the one in five with antibodies: about one in five patients with differentiated thyroid cancer have detectable anti-thyroglobulin antibodies, and this is not interference but a different mode of monitoring. Current immunometric assays tend to underestimate when antibodies are present, so the problem is not that the number needs discounting but that a reassuring number may be false; mass spectrometry is not sensitive enough; and the same passage says plainly that no thyroglobulin assay is entirely accurate when antibodies are present. A quotation box carries the guideline's verbatim sentence, "Imaging is the primary modality for monitoring in this population", a conditional recommendation with low certainty. The antibody itself then becomes the marker: followed as a trend on one assay, stable or falling counts as an indeterminate response and rising counts as a biochemical incomplete response. So for that one in five the ultrasounds are booked closer together rather than the blood drawn more often, and antibodies must be quantified every time thyroglobulin is measured, which the guideline lists as good practice and does not grade. The fifth part is the stopping point, drawn as a timeline of three stations. At six to twelve months after initial treatment, one neck ultrasound, with the timing and frequency thereafter following recurrence risk and response to therapy, listed as good practice and not graded. At five to eight years, patients at low risk who had total thyroidectomy and radioiodine and have sustained an excellent response may stop routine neck ultrasound and move to biochemical testing every one to two years, a conditional recommendation with low certainty. At ten to fifteen years, patients with a sustained excellent response need no further routine biochemical monitoring and should be regarded as having reached complete remission, listed as good practice and not graded. Beside the timeline, two conditions that travel together - low risk, and a sustained excellent response - and a note that the data are thinner for patients who had a lobectomy, for whom the guideline's wording is that if the first ultrasound is negative, one every one to three years, for five to eight years. A green band below the timeline records that "complete remission" is written into the recommendations here for the first time, and that this is the first time an ATA thyroid guideline has written down a stop. Two further cells follow: why stimulation is no longer needed before the test, from a meta-analysis of 10 studies and 1,796 patients in which undetectable high-sensitivity thyroglobulin on levothyroxine gave a negative predictive value of 99.4% (95% confidence interval 98.9 to 99.9) for excluding structural disease; and how the ultrasounds are spaced, where a suspicious node under 8 to 10 mm in short axis may be followed rather than sampled unless it grows or threatens the recurrent laryngeal nerve, trachea, oesophagus or great vessels, a conditional recommendation with low certainty, and where the guideline says the opposite of the instinct that more scans mean more safety - in patients at low risk with an excellent response, ultrasound did not find clinically meaningful disease and increased interventions through false positives. The figure ends with a red-bordered block headed "This figure will not merge the three columns into one", holding four statements: every line in the four cells belongs to its own cell alone, and reading your own report against somebody else's number is the commonest misunderstanding there is to undo in clinic; the two N/A cells in the lobectomy column are the guideline's own rather than something this figure failed to find, and cells with no line cannot be concluded from the blood test; the fourth cell, lobectomy with radioiodine, does not exist in the table because the guideline splits the reading into three columns; and "you can stop" has two conditions, low risk and a sustained excellent response, with what stops being routine cancer surveillance rather than seeing a doctor, the levothyroxine dose a separate matter, no recommendation on how often TSH should be checked findable anywhere in the 2025 text, and none supplied here in its place. A closing cell carries three sentences to say out loud with the follow-up schedule in front of you: with my extent of surgery and my radioiodine status, which line should my Tg be read against; are my anti-thyroglobulin antibodies positive or negative and, if positive, how does my follow-up change; and if I do not yet qualify to stop surveillance, please write down which condition is missing and roughly how many years are left.

g.text: ONE NUMBER, FOUR CELLS - AND TWO OF THEM ARE N/A
What the blood test means depends on how much was
removed
Thyroglobulin is not a number with one fixed normal range. Which line it has to be read against depends on exactly two things:
how much of the gland was removed, and whether radioiodine was given.
This figure crosses those two things into four cells. Two of them are written N/A in the 2025 American Thyroid Association
guideline's own table, and they are drawn here as N/A; no number is supplied in their place.
The four cells: surgical extent against radioiodine status
The guideline splits the reading of response to therapy into three columns. The lines differ between them, the lobectomy column is not the same kind of thing at all, and the
fourth cell does not exist in the table.
Total thyroidectomy
Radioiodine given
The line for "excellent response"
Tg < 0.2 ng/mL
A nonstimulated thyroglobulin - the one drawn while you are taking your tablet -
below 0.2 ng/mL, or a stimulated thyroglobulin below 1, with negative imaging.
The four response categories in the table
Excellent response
Indeterminate response
Biochemical incomplete response
Structural incomplete response
This is the column where all four categories exist and where the data are
fullest. The structural recurrence bands the guideline collects are drawn from
this column's population.
Total thyroidectomy
No radioiodine
The line for "excellent response"
Tg < 2.5 ng/mL
Same cell, next column, and the line moves from below 0.2 to below 2.5 - more
than a tenfold difference, and not a typographical error.
The four response categories in the table
Excellent response
Indeterminate response
Biochemical incomplete response
Structural incomplete response
The reason is plain: radioiodine clears the normal thyroid tissue the operation
left behind. Without it that tissue is still there, normal tissue makes this protein
too, and the baseline is simply higher. The structural recurrence figures for
this column are lower overall than for the one on its left.
Lobectomy
No radioiodine
"Excellent response" here does not look at Tg
It looks at the other lobe
Whether the contralateral lobe has a nodule, whether a biopsy of it was benign,
and whether imaging shows abnormal nodes. That is what this cell judges - not
the blood test.
The four response categories in the table
Excellent response
Indeterminate response
N/A
Biochemical incomplete response
N/A
Structural incomplete response
The two middle cells are written N/A in the table - they do not exist. On routine
thyroglobulin after lobectomy the guideline says it is not recommended
routinely, a conditional recommendation with very low certainty. Ultrasound
carries the follow-up here, not the blood test.
Lobectomy
Radioiodine given
There is no such column
The guideline splits the reading into three columns and this combination is not
one of them. This figure does not invent a line for it.
Why the lobectomy column is not the same kind of thing
This is not laziness. The systematic review that reports the three situations separately has very different numbers of patients behind each.
The 2022 systematic review, three situations reported separately
After lobectomy
4 studies, 561 patients
Total thyroidectomy without radioiodine
5 studies, 751 patients
After total thyroidectomy, before radioiodine
28 studies, 7,618 patients
“Following partial thyroidectomy, Tg measurement was not accurate for diagnosing recurrence or metastasis, or estimates were imprecise”
The verbatim conclusion of that 2022 systematic review on the first situation; it rates the quality of evidence as very low in every situation.
The 30 ng/mL cutoff was not adopted in 2025
A cutoff of 30 ng/mL after lobectomy was indeed proposed in 2016, in
a single-centre cohort of 507 patients, none of whom had radioiodine.
The 2025 edition did not adopt it. So if someone reads your report
against the number 30, ask first which document that line comes
from.
Even in the two left-hand columns, the first result is not the
verdict
In a cohort of 299 patients, all of whom had total thyroidectomy and remnant
ablation and no further treatment afterwards, only 58% had reached their
nadir by six months, and 75% by twelve.
A first result that is not low enough does not settle the matter.
Four response categories, each with its own recurrence rate
The guideline requires response to therapy to be described with these four categories: a strong recommendation with moderate certainty. The structural recurrence bands
below are for adults with differentiated thyroid cancer after total thyroidectomy and radioiodine - that is, the people in the top left cell.
Excellent response
No clinical, biochemical or imaging evidence of disease
Excellent response, and low risk from the start
The separate figure given in the same passage
Indeterminate response
Something non-specific found, neither clearly benign nor malignant; stable or falling antibodies count here too
Biochemical incomplete response
Abnormal Tg or rising antibodies with no lesion found
Structural incomplete response
Local or distant metastases visible on imaging
Visible on imaging
The corresponding figures in the column without radioiodine are lower overall. These four cells describe where you are now, not where you were placed at the
beginning.
This classification rewrites the category you were put in at the start
588 patients, median follow-up 7 years (total thyroidectomy and remnant
ablation, on the three-tier system of the time)
Persistent structural disease or recurrence as first classified
Low risk at the start
Intermediate risk
High risk
Re-classified after an excellent response in the first two years
Low risk
Intermediate risk
High risk
506 patients, median follow-up 10 years (total thyroidectomy and ablation again)
A result in the same direction
Low risk
Intermediate risk
High risk
After an excellent response
Those reaching an excellent response
Neither set matches the figures in the sister article on staging (1.5%, 5.4%, 25%), because the endpoint definitions and the cohorts differ. The same risk category gives different
percentages in different studies, and that is itself why the category you start in is not a verdict.
The one in five with antibodies: not "interference", a different mode of monitoring
About one in five patients with differentiated thyroid cancer have detectable anti-thyroglobulin antibodies. Many are told the antibodies interfere and the number should be
discounted a little. That is not right.
The problem is not a discount; it is that a reassuring number may be false
Current immunometric assays tend to underestimate in the presence of antibodies, so the problem is not a discount; mass spectrometry is not sensitive
enough.
The same passage of the guideline puts it plainly: no thyroglobulin assay is entirely accurate when antibodies are present.
“Imaging is the primary modality for monitoring in this population”
2025 American Thyroid Association guideline; conditional recommendation, low certainty.
So the antibody itself becomes the marker
Followed as a trend on one assay, stable or falling
counts as an indeterminate response
Followed as a trend on one assay, rising
counts as a biochemical incomplete response
If you are one of that one in five, your ultrasounds are booked closer together rather than your blood drawn more often. Antibodies must be quantified every time
thyroglobulin is measured - the guideline lists this as good practice and does not grade it.
The first time an ATA thyroid guideline has written down a stop
Every previous edition said how to follow patients and never said on which day following could end.
Six to twelve months after initial treatment
One neck ultrasound; the timing and frequency after that follow your
recurrence risk and your response to therapy. The guideline lists this as good
practice and does not grade it.
Five to eight years
Patients at low risk who had total thyroidectomy and radioiodine and have
sustained an excellent response may stop routine neck ultrasound, and move to
biochemical testing every one to two years. Conditional recommendation, low
certainty.
Ten to fifteen years
Patients with a sustained excellent response for ten to fifteen years need no
further routine biochemical monitoring and should be regarded as having
reached complete remission. The guideline lists this as good practice and does
not grade it.
Two conditions, and they travel together
Low risk.
And a sustained excellent response.
The data are thinner for patients who had a lobectomy
The guideline says so itself, and its wording for them is that if the first
ultrasound is negative, one every one to three years, for five to eight years.
"Complete remission" is written into the recommendations here for the first time.
Why stimulation is no longer needed before the test
A meta-analysis of 10 studies and 1,796 patients found that when high-sensitivity
thyroglobulin is undetectable on levothyroxine, the negative predictive value for
excluding structural disease is 99.4% (95% confidence interval 98.9 to 99.9).
How the ultrasounds are spaced, and when a node need not be
biopsied
A suspicious node does not automatically have to be sampled: one under 8 to
10 mm in short axis may be followed instead, unless it grows or threatens
the recurrent laryngeal nerve, trachea, oesophagus or great vessels
(conditional recommendation, low certainty).
Against the instinct that more scans mean more safety, the guideline says the
opposite: in patients at low risk with an excellent response, ultrasound did
not find clinically meaningful disease and increased the number of
interventions through false positives.
This figure will not merge the three columns into one
Every line in the four cells belongs to its own cell alone. Reading your own report against somebody else's number is the commonest misunderstanding
there is to undo in clinic.
The two N/A cells in the lobectomy column are the guideline's own, not something this figure failed to find. Those two cells have no line, so those two
cells cannot be concluded from the blood test.
The fourth cell - lobectomy with radioiodine - does not exist in the table, because the guideline splits the reading into three columns.
"You can stop" has two conditions: low risk, and a sustained excellent response. What stops is routine cancer surveillance, not seeing a doctor. How
the levothyroxine dose is adjusted is a separate matter; no recommendation on how often TSH should be checked could be found anywhere in the 2025
text, and this figure does not supply one either.
Three sentences to say out loud with the follow-up schedule in front of you
"With my extent of surgery and my radioiodine status, which line should my Tg be read against?"
"Are my anti-thyroglobulin antibodies positive or negative? If positive, how does my follow-up change?"
"If I do not yet qualify to stop surveillance, please write down which condition is missing and roughly how many years are left."
Schematic, redrawn from the 2025 American Thyroid Association guidelines for differentiated thyroid cancer, the 2022 systematic review of thyroglobulin
measurement after surgery without radioiodine, the 2016 dynamic risk stratification cohort of Momesso and colleagues, the 2012 cohort on the natural fall of
thyroglobulin, the 2010 re-stratification study of Tuttle and colleagues, the 2012 cohort on biochemical incomplete response and the 2019 meta-analysis of
high-sensitivity thyroglobulin; not reproduced from the figures of the original papers. The cohorts, designs and endpoints of the underlying studies differ, so the
data points must not be compared directly.
